strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents an intuitive idea: diffusion policies can model multimodal exploratory behavior better than conventional Gaussian or finite-skill policies.
The evaluation spans three Maze2d environments and 16 URLB tasks across four domains, with 10 seeds and aggregate metrics with bootstrap confidence intervals.
Maze visualizations provide compelling qualitative evidence that the learned diffusion policy reproduces a broader portion of the collected behavior distribution.
The paper includes useful ablations of the score reward, Q-learning method, and number of diffusion sampling steps.
weaknesses: The central intrinsic-reward justification is not sound. Equation 6 provides an upper bound on negative log likelihood, so a large denoising loss does not establish low data probability. Dropping the diffusion weighting further weakens the connection. The reward can therefore measure model error or optimization difficulty rather than novelty.

The fine-tuning formulation contains serious technical inconsistencies. The paper alternates between treating the diffusion network output as a noise predictor and as a score without the necessary scaling, while Equations 12/30 define the CEP output as a scalar energy-related quantity but Equations 13/31 directly add it to a vector noise prediction instead of using its action gradient. This leaves the implemented policy update mathematically under-specified.

Theorem 3.1 analyzes exact policy evaluation and exact distributional policy improvement, not the practical IQL, finite-sample CEP, and score-distillation procedure. Its convergence-to-optimality statement is asserted only under unspecified regularity conditions, and the proof around Equations 22–24 contains a mismatched equality involving F and the Q-function difference.

The empirical design does not cleanly attribute gains to the proposed ideas. On URLB, EDP combines RND with the score reward and uses a substantially different IQL/CEP diffusion fine-tuning pipeline, whereas baselines are fine-tuned with DDPG. The main ablation is restricted to four Quadruped tasks and does not provide a fully matched comparison across the benchmark.

Several relevant unsupervised-RL baselines are absent, including stronger state-entropy or representation-based approaches such as APT/ProtoRL, APS, and METRA. Comparisons to recent online diffusion-policy training methods are also missing.

The results are less uniformly strong than the presentation suggests: EDP is excellent on Quadruped and Jaco but substantially trails CIC or BeCL on several Walker tasks and does not dominate Hopper. Per-task results report only means and apparently select the best policy checkpoint, without uncertainty or a clearly specified checkpoint-selection protocol.

Reproducibility and efficiency evidence are insufficient. Important hyperparameters and implementation details—including the intrinsic-reward coefficient and normalization, diffusion architecture and training schedule, beta, and CEP/IQL settings—are omitted. No wall-clock, memory, or interaction-throughput comparison supports the efficiency claims despite the considerable diffusion-training and sampling overhead.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: obtaining expressive policies that both explore effectively during reward-free pre-training and adapt quickly to downstream tasks.

Using a diffusion model to represent multimodal exploratory behavior is intuitively well motivated, and the distinction between a fast Gaussian behavior policy and an expressive diffusion policy is practically sensible.
The experiments cover three maze layouts and 16 continuous-control tasks, use 10 seeds for URLB, and report aggregate metrics with bootstrap confidence intervals.
The maze visualizations provide useful qualitative evidence that the diffusion policy reproduces more of the replay-buffer diversity than Gaussian and discrete-skill policies.
weaknesses: The central intrinsic-reward justification is unsound. Equation 6 gives only an upper bound on negative log-likelihood; a large denoising loss does not establish that a transition has low probability. Per-sample denoising error can instead reflect irreducible conditional ambiguity, model misspecification, noise level, or optimization error. Thus the claimed interpretation of R_score as visitation novelty is not theoretically supported.

The practical diffusion fine-tuning equations appear dimensionally inconsistent. Equations 12 and 30 define f as a scalar positive classifier/energy quantity used inside a logarithm, while Equations 13 and 31 add it directly to a vector-valued noise predictor. The preceding derivation requires an action gradient of the intermediate energy, together with the appropriate score/noise scaling, but the stated distillation objective uses neither. This leaves a central component mathematically incorrect or insufficiently specified.

Theorem 3.1 does not validate the implemented method. It assumes exact policy improvement and exact evaluation of Q^{pi_n}, whereas the algorithm uses replay-buffer IQL, approximate CEP guidance, and learned score distillation. Appendix B's IQL target is ordinary reward-based IQL and does not explicitly implement the KL-regularized Q definition used by the theorem. The convergence-to-global-optimum claim is asserted under unspecified regularity conditions rather than established.

The downstream comparison is substantially confounded: baselines are fine-tuned with DDPG, while EDP uses a specialized IQL/CEP diffusion procedure. Consequently, the results cannot determine whether gains arise from better unsupervised pre-training, the expressive policy class, or the stronger/different fine-tuning algorithm. Essential controls include scratch diffusion training, diffusion behavior cloning with RND data, common fine-tuning algorithms, and contemporary diffusion-RL baselines.

EDP combines RND and the proposed score reward, but the principal exploration comparisons are against standalone RND and other methods. The relevant ablation is shown only on four Quadruped downstream tasks, not on maze coverage or the full 16-task suite. This is insufficient to support the claim that the score reward itself drives the reported exploration advantage.

Empirical reporting is incomplete. Per-task uncertainty and statistical tests are absent; Table 1 reports the mean return of the 'best policy,' which introduces unclear checkpoint-selection bias; computational cost and wall-clock efficiency are not reported despite diffusion sampling and repeated model fitting; and robustness to reward scaling, beta, diffusion steps during training, and the RND/score mixture is not studied.

Reproducibility is weak: key details such as architectures, diffusion schedule, reward normalization and mixture coefficient, beta, CEP sample count, IQL expectile, update ratios, optimizer settings, and evaluation/checkpoint protocol are missing. There are also notable presentation errors, including an incorrect DDPG citation and inconsistent partition-function exponents.

Overall, the idea is promising, but the mathematical inconsistency in the stated fine-tuning algorithm, unsupported novelty interpretation, and heavily confounded evaluation prevent the central claims from being established at a top-tier standard.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in unsupervised RL and offers an intuitive motivation: diffusion policies can preserve multimodal behaviors that unimodal Gaussian policies may discard.

Using diffusion-model denoising error as an intrinsic exploration signal is a potentially useful idea, and combining exploration with an expressive pretrained policy creates a coherent two-stage framework.
The evaluation covers three maze environments and 16 URLB downstream tasks, uses 10 seeds per task, and reports aggregate metrics with bootstrap confidence intervals.

The maze visualizations and coverage curves provide clear evidence that EDP explores broadly and that its pretrained diffusion policy reproduces more of the collected behavioral diversity than the selected baselines.
The RND-only and alternative-Q-learning ablations provide some evidence that both the score reward and the proposed fine-tuning choices contribute to performance.
weaknesses: The practical diffusion fine-tuning equations appear technically inconsistent. The paper defines the diffusion network as a vector-valued noise predictor, while CEP learns a scalar positive energy through the contrastive objective in Eq. 12. Equations 13 and 31 then directly subtract this scalar energy from the noise prediction. Guided diffusion instead requires a gradient of the energy with respect to the noisy action, together with the appropriate noise-schedule scaling. The appendix itself states a result involving the gradient of f, making the stated distillation objective dimensionally and conceptually invalid. This affects a central component and prevents faithful reproduction.

The theoretical result does not establish the correctness of the implemented algorithm. The theorem concerns exact evaluation of Q under the current policy followed by an exact KL-regularized policy update, whereas the practical method substitutes IQL and CEP/distillation without bounding their approximation errors. The IQL objective shown does not explicitly implement the KL-regularized Bellman evaluation used by the theorem. The final convergence-to-optimality claim is also asserted only under unspecified regularity conditions.

The interpretation of the score reward is overstated. A diffusion denoising objective supplies an upper bound on negative log likelihood; maximizing a per-sample upper bound does not necessarily maximize novelty or low data probability. Moreover, the conditional model estimates action likelihood given a state rather than the joint state-action visitation density, so it does not directly measure whether a state itself is rarely visited. High error can also reflect model approximation error or stochasticity rather than epistemic novelty.

The main URLB comparison confounds pretraining quality, policy class, and fine-tuning algorithm: baselines use Gaussian DDPG fine-tuning, while EDP uses a diffusion policy with IQL and guided distillation. The RND-only EDP ablation helps, but it is reported only on the four Quadruped tasks and lacks uncertainty estimates. Applying the same expressive policy and fine-tuning pipeline to alternative pretraining objectives across all domains is needed to support the central attribution.

EDP is not uniformly state of the art: it substantially trails CIC or BeCL on several Walker tasks and trails multiple methods on some Hopper tasks. The aggregate figure suggests competitiveness rather than a decisive overall advantage, while the text sometimes claims significant superiority without reporting pairwise statistical tests.
The baseline set omits relevant strong unsupervised-RL methods such as METRA, despite discussing METRA in related work. This weakens the empirical positioning against the current state of the art.

Important evidence is incomplete: Table 1 provides means without variances, the ablations cover only one domain, there is no sensitivity analysis for the reward mixture or KL temperature, and computational cost and wall-clock efficiency are not reported despite diffusion sampling and repeated model training being central practical concerns.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of detailed architectures, optimization hyperparameters, reward normalization and weighting, CEP sample count, IQL settings, and training schedules in the manuscript. The paper refers to supplementary code, but the written specification is not sufficient to reconstruct the method, especially given the inconsistent fine-tuning equations.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem and presents a coherent two-stage framework combining diffusion-based state-density estimation, an efficient Gaussian behavior policy, and downstream policy adaptation.

The empirical study is broad: seven maze environments, four URLB domains with 16 downstream tasks, comparisons against numerous exploration, skill-discovery, and diffusion-policy baselines, and 10 seeds per setting.

The reported results are strong, particularly for maze coverage and URLB aggregate metrics, and the paper includes learning curves, confidence intervals, several ablations, hyperparameters, and compute information.
The manuscript is generally well organized and explicitly acknowledges the additional computation and continuous-action limitation.
weaknesses: The central theoretical motivation is not convincing. Theorem 3.1 assumes that occupancy measures of all deterministic policies are independent uniform samples from the probability simplex. This highly artificial assumption is neither mild nor connected to the dynamics of a fixed MDP, so the theorem does not establish that maximum-entropy exploration generally requires a diffusion policy.

The intrinsic-reward derivation is technically under-supported. Equation 7 invokes a weighted diffusion ELBO but then discards the timestep weights; the resulting unweighted denoising error in Equation 8 is therefore not generally an upper bound or calibrated estimate of negative log density. Denoising error can also reflect model misspecification rather than state novelty, and the paper provides no calibration analysis or comparison with alternative expressive density estimators.

The diffusion fine-tuning equations appear inconsistent. Equation 13 trains a positive scalar function through a contrastive log-ratio objective, while Equation 14 directly subtracts that function from the vector noise prediction. The appendix instead states that a gradient of the learned energy yields score guidance, yet Equation 36 again uses the function itself. This scalar/vector and energy/score mismatch makes the implemented algorithm unclear and potentially invalid as written.

Theorem 3.2 concerns exact policy evaluation and exact energy-tilted policy updates, whereas the practical method uses approximate IQL, learned CEP guidance, finite-sample distillation, and online replay. IQL's support conservatism is not shown to implement the stated reference-policy KL penalty. Thus, the theorem does not establish improvement or convergence for Algorithm 2, and the final optimal-convergence argument is only asserted under unspecified regularity conditions.

The key causal claim that diffusion modeling is responsible for the gains lacks decisive ablations. There is no comparison against similarly expressive non-diffusion density models, weighted versus unweighted diffusion rewards, simpler prediction-error bonuses under matched capacity, or a compute/parameter-matched alternative. The paper also does not quantify wall-clock or sample-throughput costs against baselines despite emphasizing efficiency.

Reporting has additional weaknesses: per-task URLB results omit uncertainty and are described as the return of the 'best policy,' leaving checkpoint selection and possible selection bias unclear; some relevant modern URL methods are cited but not evaluated; and the diffusion-policy variant remains worse than the Gaussian-policy variant, weakening the claimed downstream benefit of diffusion policies themselves. Overall, the promising empirical results do not overcome the substantial soundness and attribution gaps.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and presents an intuitively appealing combination of diffusion-based density modeling, intrinsic-reward exploration, and downstream policy adaptation.

The empirical results are promising: ExDM achieves substantially higher coverage in the harder Maze2d environments and strong aggregate URLB performance. The use of 10 seeds and stratified-bootstrap intervals for aggregate metrics is commendable.

The evaluation includes numerous exploration and skill-discovery baselines, multiple continuous-control domains, several downstream tasks, and some ablations. The paper is generally organized clearly and reports approximate computational cost.
weaknesses: The central intrinsic-reward justification is unsound. The denoising loss is only part of an upper bound on negative log likelihood, and the paper discards the time-dependent weights. Maximizing a potentially loose upper bound does not imply maximizing state novelty or entropy: high reward may reflect model approximation error, optimization difficulty, or observation noise rather than low visitation density. No empirical density-calibration analysis validates the proposed interpretation.

Theorem 3.1 relies on the highly artificial assumption that occupancy distributions of all deterministic policies are independent uniform samples from the probability simplex. In a fixed MDP they are strongly coupled through shared dynamics and the initial-state distribution, and many policies can induce identical occupancies. Calling these assumptions mild is misleading. Moreover, showing that an entropy-maximizing policy may be stochastic does not establish that it requires a diffusion policy or even a complex policy class.

The fine-tuning formulation contains major mathematical ambiguities. Equation 13 treats f as a positive scalar classifier or energy, while Equation 14 directly subtracts f from a vector-valued noise prediction. The appendix instead invokes the action gradient of f, and even there the contrastive objective would naturally identify a log-gradient rather than the stated gradient. Consequently, the practical diffusion-policy update is dimensionally inconsistent and cannot be reproduced from the manuscript.

Theorem 3.2 does not justify the implemented method. Its global-convergence claim is concluded only by asserting unspecified regularity conditions, and the proof around Equations 27–30 contains a mismatched equality involving F. More fundamentally, the theorem assumes exact policy improvement and exact Q evaluation, whereas the algorithm uses approximate IQL, finite replay data, learned CEP guidance, and score distillation; no error analysis connects these approximations to the claimed monotonic improvement.

The experiments lack the component ablations needed to support the paper's causal claims. There is no comparison against a Gaussian or other density estimator, an appropriately weighted diffusion likelihood, a simpler prediction-error novelty signal, or ExDM without the action diffusion policy. Because exploration actions are generated by the Gaussian behavior policy, the action diffusion model does not itself improve exploration, and the strong Gaussian-policy downstream results cannot substantiate claims about diffusion-policy initialization.

Important evaluation and reproducibility details are missing, including beta, CEP sample count K, IQL expectile, update-to-data ratios, intrinsic-reward normalization, state preprocessing, and state-model architecture. Diffusion fine-tuning is shown only through aggregate plots, without per-task results or sufficient protocol details. Reporting the mean return of the 'best policy' also leaves checkpoint selection and possible selection bias unclear.

The claims of efficiency and broad superiority are overstated. Results primarily establish sample-based coverage on simple custom two-dimensional mazes and performance on one continuous-control benchmark, while the additional diffusion computation is substantial and no wall-clock or compute-matched comparison is provided. The diffusion-policy variant is also explicitly worse than the Gaussian-policy variant.

Overall, the empirical signal is interesting, but the theoretical arguments do not establish the stated conclusions, the central fine-tuning update is inconsistently specified, and the ablations are insufficient to attribute the improvements to the proposed diffusion mechanisms. These are substantial issues rather than minor presentation gaps.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and relevant idea: using a diffusion state model's denoising error as an intrinsic reward while separately learning a diffusion policy from the heterogeneous replay buffer.

The empirical results are promising. ExDM achieves strong state coverage across seven Maze2d environments and improves aggregate downstream performance on 16 URLB tasks, with comparisons against ten unsupervised-RL methods and four diffusion-policy baselines.

The evaluation uses 10 seeds, reports uncertainty for maze coverage and stratified-bootstrap intervals for aggregate URLB metrics, and includes useful studies of pre-training duration, critic choice, and diffusion sampling steps.

The distinction between an efficient Gaussian behavior policy for data collection and an expressive diffusion policy for modeling collected behavior is practically motivated. The paper is generally well organized and discusses computational and discrete-action limitations.
No substantial ethical concern is apparent for the presented benchmark research.
weaknesses: The connection between the proposed reward and state novelty is insufficiently justified. Equation 7 requires timestep-dependent ELBO weights, but the method drops them; per-sample denoising error can also reflect model approximation error and local distribution complexity rather than low state density. No empirical calibration against actual visitation density is provided.

The diffusion-policy fine-tuning formulation contains a serious mathematical inconsistency. The CEP model in Equations 13 and 35 is a scalar positive energy estimator used inside a logarithm, and the appendix states that its gradient estimates the energy guidance. Equations 14 and 36 instead directly subtract this scalar from a vector-valued noise/score predictor, without the required gradient or noise-to-score scaling. As written, the objective is dimensionally and algorithmically unclear.

Theorem 3.1 relies on the occupancy measures of all deterministic policies being independent uniform samples from the probability simplex. This is not a mild assumption for an MDP: the measures share the same dynamics and initial distribution and are strongly dependent and constrained. The theorem therefore offers little support for the claimed necessity of expressive diffusion policies in realistic URL problems.

Theorem 3.2 essentially concerns exact regularized policy iteration with exact value functions and exact policy updates. The practical procedure uses approximate IQL, finite-sample CEP, and score distillation, so its monotonic-improvement and convergence guarantees do not apply to the implemented algorithm. The final optimal-convergence argument is also only asserted under unspecified regularity conditions.

The ablations do not isolate the paper's central claims. In particular, there is no comparison against a Gaussian or other density estimator using the same prediction-error reward, no weighted-ELBO or likelihood-based reward comparison, and no direct evidence that the learned diffusion policy represents the replay distribution better than a simpler policy. The reported diffusion policy also performs worse downstream than ExDM's Gaussian policy.

Several important implementation details are absent, including the KL temperature beta, CEP sample count K, IQL expectile, update ratios, intrinsic-reward normalization, and the number of noise/timestep samples used to estimate each reward. This limits reproducibility despite the claim that code is supplied.

The experimental breadth is good but remains confined to state-based continuous-control benchmarks, and relevant recent strong URL methods such as METRA are discussed but not evaluated. Per-task URLB uncertainty is omitted, and Table 3 reports the mean return of the best policy rather than clearly specifying a fixed final-checkpoint evaluation. Overall, the empirical promise is substantial, but the central technical inconsistencies and missing diagnostic ablations place the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.
